courses.subject: CPSC
courses.title: Introduction to Programming Lecture
courses.description: Introduction computer science and computer programming, including designing programs; sequential execution; variables, assignment and arithmetic; control flow, Boolean logic, selection and loops; input/output; functions; debugging; practical applications; and development methodologies. (50-minute lecture)

courses.subject: CPSC
courses.title: Introduction to Programming Lab
courses.description: Introduction to computer science and computer programming, including designing programs; sequential execution; variables, assignment and arithmetic; control flow, Boolean logic, selection and loops; input/output; functions; debugging; practical applications; and development methodologies.

courses.subject: CPSC
courses.title: Object Oriented Programming Lecture
courses.description: The object-oriented programming paradigm, including classes, objects, member variables and functions; exceptions, inheritance, templates, encapsulation, decoupling and class design best practices. Advanced program design, including iterators, operator overloading, recursion and dynamic memory allocation (50-minute lecture).

courses.subject: CPSC
courses.title: Object-Oriented Programming Lab
courses.description: Apply object-oriented programming concepts, including classes, objects, member variables and functions; exceptions, inheritance, templates, encapsulation, decoupling and class design best practices. Advanced program design, including iterators, operator overloading, recursion and dynamic memory allocation.

sections.instructor: Paul Salvador Inventado, Akshay Bhagwat Nimse

courses.subject: CPSC
courses.title: Data Structures
courses.description: Classical data structures: vector, linked list, stack, queue, binary search tree, and graph representations. Worst-case analysis, amortized analysis, and big-O notation. Object-oriented and recursive implementation of data structures. Self-resizing vectors and self-balancing trees. Empirical performance measurement.

courses.subject: CPSC
courses.title: Python Programming
courses.description: Concepts of computing, domain-specific problem solving with computing technologies. Methodologies, tools and the application development process. Variables, expressions, control flow, functions, standard libraries, packages, data structures, files, modularization, integration. Develop functional applications. (2 hours lecture, 2 hours lab per week)

courses.subject: ENGL
courses.title: Beginning College Writing
courses.description: Introduction to the fundamentals of expository prose. Grammatical and basic rhetorical concepts and practices necessary for successful college writing. Placement to be determined by multiple measures. Instructional fee.

courses.subject: ENGL
courses.title: Preparatory College Writing
courses.description: Practice and instruction in college-level writing. Writing, revision, grammar, rhetorical and research skills necessary for success in ENGL 101. Enrollment determined by appropriate placement assessment. (ENGL 101P and ESE 101P are the same course.)

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: World Civilizations to the 16th Century
courses.description: Development of Western and non-Western civilizations from their origins to the 16th century.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: World Civilizations Since the 16th Century
courses.description: Development of Western and non-Western civilizations from the 16th century to the present.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: United States to 1877
courses.description: Political, social, economic and cultural development of the United States to 1877. Old World background, rise of the new nation, sectional problems, the Civil War and Reconstruction.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: United States Since 1877
courses.description: U.S. history from the late 19th century to the present. Economic transformation, political reform movements, social, cultural and intellectual changes and the role of the United States in world affairs.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Survey of American History
courses.description: American history from prehistoric times (before 1492) to the present according to chronological time periods. Basic themes that pervade the entire sweep of the nation's history. Satisfies state requirement in U.S. History.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Historical Thinking
courses.description: Nature of history, history of historical thought and history's relationship to the humanities and social sciences. Seminar required of all history majors. History majors must earn at a "C" (2.0) or better.

courses.subject: HIST
courses.title: Historical Writing
courses.description: Research, writing and library usage (including computer-assisted bibliographic searches) as related to history. Meets the classroom portion of the upper-division writing requirement for history majors. Seminar required of all history majors. History majors must earn at least a "C" (2.0) in this course.

courses.subject: KNES
courses.title: Physical Conditioning
courses.description: Performance courses are instructional. Beginning, intermediate and advanced sections are offered for most performance courses. Students who already possess proficiency in an activity should consider the course chosen from the standpoint of the level of skill development that may be encountered, standards of proficiency expected and their own ability level. Initial assessment and determination will be made by the course instructor. May be repeated for a maximum of 6 units.

courses.title: Fitness Walking
courses.description: Performance courses are instructional. Beginning, intermediate and advanced sections are offered for most performance courses. courses.subject: KNES
courses.title: Aquatic Adaptation
courses.description: Provide non-swimmers with basic water-comfort skills. Identified non-swimmers (self or by instructor) are those who may be uncomfortable in the water or have never received formal swim instruction.

courses.subject: KNES
courses.title: Beginning Swimming

Students who already possess proficiency in an activity should consider the course chosen from the standpoint of the level of skill development that may be encountered, standards of proficiency expected and their own ability level. Initial assessment and determination will be made by the course instructor. May be repeated for a maximum of 6 units..

Students who already possess proficiency in an activity should consider the course chosen from the standpoint of the level of skill development that may be encountered, standards of proficiency expected and their own ability level. courses.subject: KNES
courses.title: Beginning Bowling
courses.description: Performance courses are instructional. Beginning, intermediate and advanced sections are offered for most performance courses. Students who already possess proficiency in an activity should consider the course chosen from the standpoint of the level of skill development that may be encountered, standards of proficiency expected and their own ability level. Initial assessment and determination will be made by the course instructor. May be taken for credit for a maximum of six units.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Mathematics For Liberal Arts Supplement
courses.description: Order of operations, calculator functions, fractions, percent, linear equations, inequalities, quadratics, exponential and logarithmic functions, sequences and series. Degree credit not awarded. (MATH 10S and ESM 10S are the same course.)

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Elementary Statistics Supplement
courses.description: Order of operations, mathematical expressions and functions. Conversion between fractions, proportions, decimals, percentages and probabilities. Average rate of change, equation of a line and intersection of two lines. Mathematical and statistical word problems. Data entry and use of statistical software. (MATH 20S and ESM 20S are the same course.)

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Differential and Integral Calculus Essentials
courses.description: Properties of functions. Rules and applications of limits, derivatives, antiderivatives. Integrals. Fundamental theorem of calculus. Differential equations. Requires department approval.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Integral Calculus and Differential Equations
courses.description: Introduction to solving differential equations via the Laplace transform, series solutions and Fourier series. Techniques of integration, applications of integration, improper integrals.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Introduction to Computational Linear Algebra
courses.description: Introduction to linear algebra and computation with applications. Linear algebra: Euclidean spaces, matrices, matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Computation: variables, functions, conditionals, loops and plotting.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Mathematics for Liberal Arts Students
courses.description: Survey of traditional and contemporary topics in mathematics, such as elementary logic, counting techniques, probability, statistics, and the mathematics of the social sciences. For non-science majors.

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: College Algebra
courses.description: For students planning to take MATH 130 or MATH 135. Equations, inequalities, and systems of equations. Properties of functions and their graphs, including polynomial functions, rational functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, with applications. Sequences and series. If both MATH 115 and MATH 125 are taken and the student receives a "C" or better in both courses, then the second course is the course that receives credit. If the student only succeeds in one of the two courses, then credit is given for the course successfully completed.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy
courses.description: Nature, methods and some of the main problems of philosophy. Primarily for freshmen and sophomores. Not a prerequisite for advanced courses.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Meaning, Purpose, and the Good Life
courses.description: Introduction to Western and Eastern approaches to perennial topics in philosophy concerning human flourishing and the nature of persons. Questions considered include, "What is happiness?" "What is the good life?" "Does life have meaning and purpose?" and "What is a person?"

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Critical Thinking
courses.description: Developing non-mathematical critical reasoning skills, including recognition of arguments, argument evaluation and construction of arguments.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Introduction to Logic
courses.description: Logical structure of language and correct reasoning: deduction, induction, scientific reasoning and informal fallacies.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: Video Games, the Arts and Philosophy
courses.description: Introduction to art, visual art, games and game theory. Aesthetics of games and interactive visual media. Epistemic and moral relations of virtual worlds to reality. Ultimate value of game-play and visual arts to life's meaning and purpose.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: History of Philosophy: Greek Philosophy
courses.description: Origins of Western philosophy and its development through Socrates, Plato and Aristotle.

courses.subject: PHIL
courses.title: History of Philosophy: Rationalism and Empiricism
geCategories: Explorations in the Arts or Humanities
courses.description: Rationalism of Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz, and the empiricism of Locke, Berkeley and Hume.
